headline: Weinstein gets 15 years. He's already served six.
summary: A Manhattan judge sentenced Harvey Weinstein Wednesday to 15 years for sexually assaulting Miriam Haley, a TV production assistant, in 2006. A jury convicted him in 2020. New York's top court threw that out in 2024, and a second jury convicted him again. He has already served six years. Haley told the court: "It's a life sentence for me."

cover_question.q: Why did they try him twice?

cover_answer: An unfair trial means do it over. Not go free.
table_question: If a referee got a call wrong, should the whole game be replayed?

5-7.script: A man who used to make movies hurt a woman a long time ago, and yesterday a judge said he has to stay in prison for 15 years. The first trial got mixed up, so they did it over, the way you replay a point when the rules get muddled. He's been in prison six years already. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: A replayed point, then a settled ending. A five-year-old takes the one vivid piece for the whole story, so pick it for them.
5-7.why_long: A five-year-old takes one vivid piece for the whole event, so the script hands them a replayed point and a settled ending. Cantor found that what frightens this age is the near and the concrete, so the man stays far away and in prison. Expect "did he say sorry?" He said sorry for her pain and still says he didn't do it.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: In 2020 a jury found Harvey Weinstein guilty of assaulting Miriam Haley. In 2024 New York's top court threw it out: the jury had heard from women whose cases weren't on trial. Against the rules. So they replayed it, like a referee ordering a do-over, and a second jury said guilty. Wednesday: 15 years.
8-12.why: Guilty, thrown out, guilty again: a chain in order. The replay is a rule they know.
8-12.why_long: This age tests whether rules apply to everyone, so the script runs the chain in order: guilty, thrown out because the jury heard too much, guilty again. The replay is a rule they know, and it shows fairness runs both ways: a clean trial, and the verdict stands. Expect "was the first jury wrong?" No. It heard what it shouldn't have.

13-17.script: If a trial was unfair to the defendant, is the fix a new trial or freedom? New York's top court picked a new trial for Harvey Weinstein, and a second jury convicted him again. Then: Miriam Haley testified twice and called it "a life sentence for me." Is that a price the system should ask of her?
13-17.why: Two true things: an unfair trial, and guilty anyway. Then Haley's cost.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things: the first trial was unfair to Weinstein, and the second found him guilty. The script hands them both, then Haley's cost, so fairness has a person in it. Kuhn's point is that argument is practised, so let them argue for the retrial first. Expect "would you have testified again?" Answer honestly.

5-7.q: Is he going to get out?
5-7.a: Not for a long time. A judge gave him 15 years, and he has already been in prison for six.

8-12.q: Why did they have to do the trial twice?
8-12.a: The first jury heard stories that weren't charged. Do-over.

8-12.q: Did she have to tell it again?
8-12.a: Yes. Twice at trial, and again in court on Wednesday.

13-17.q: Why did they try him twice?
13-17.a: A redo, not a free pass. The second jury said guilty too.
Prosecutors wanted 20, his lawyers three more. Judge said 15.
